p: The Latin adds a third city, On; Charles traced it to the Greek Exodus 1:11.

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902

why: Charles 1902 judged the Latin's "and On" an addition, probably made under the influence of the Greek Exodus 1:11. The Hebrew of Exodus 1:11 and the Ge'ez name two cities.

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902

why: The Ge'ez is followed. The Latin omission (noted in Charles 1902) changes little: Egypt still rebuilds its walls.

p: The Ge'ez has "her Hebrew women"; the Latin has "maid," as Exodus 2:5 has "her slave woman."

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902

why: Charles 1902, following Dillmann, judged the Ge'ez a mistranslation of the Greek ἄβραις, "maids," read as "Hebrew women"; the Latin's singular matches the Hebrew, Samaritan, Greek and Latin texts of Exodus 2:5. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez as it stands and explains the likely slip in a note.

p: VanderKam prints the whole clause in square brackets; Charles marks only "to her" as restored, from the Latin and Exodus 2:8.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), in square brackets
readings.en: And she said to her, Go.

readings.w: Charles 1902's Ethiopic, before he restored "to her" from the Latin and Exodus 2:8

why: The transcription of VanderKam's edition used here brackets "And she said to her, Go," but does not explain the brackets. Charles 1902 prints the clause and marks only "to her" as his restoration ("Restored from the Latin and Exod. ii. 8"). The answer is needed for the story (47:8 says "So she went") and stands in Exodus 2:8 ("'Go,' Pharaoh's daughter told her"), so the Plain English Translation keeps it with "to her."

p: The Ge'ez and the Latin say "Pharaoh's house." Charles corrected it to "Pharaoh's daughter," as in Exodus 2:10.
why: Every witness read here has "house," so the Plain English Translation keeps it. Charles 1902 argued that the Greek translator misread Hebrew bat, "daughter," as bayit, "house": Exodus 2:10 has "she took him to Pharaoh's daughter," and the next words, "you became her son," need a woman. The correction is attractive but is a guess about the lost Hebrew.

p: Charles's English adds "yesterday," as in the Greek Exodus 2:14 and Acts 7:28.

readings.en: as thou killedst the Egyptian yesterday
readings.plain: as you killed the Egyptian yesterday

why: VanderKam's Ge'ez has no "yesterday," and neither does the Hebrew of Exodus 2:14. Charles's English has it, as does Acts 7:28 ("the same way you killed that Egyptian yesterday"); his note does not say where he took it from, so the Ge'ez is followed.

p: The Ge'ez says "there." The Latin says "in the land of Midian."

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: lived in the land of Midian

why: Charles 1902 restored "in the land of Midian" from the Latin and Exodus 2:15. The Ge'ez "there" is followed: it has no place named before it, but the reader of Exodus 2:15 knows where Moses went, and the Latin may have filled the name in.

a: on the road, at the shelter
p: The Ge'ez is hard here. The Latin says "at the lodging-place," like Exodus 4:24; one manuscript says "at the Feast of Booths."

readings.en: on the road, at the ... of shelter
readings.plain: on the road, at the shelter

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.orig: in via in qua praeteristi eum in refectione
readings.en: in the way in which you passed him, at the lodging-place
readings.plain: on the road where you passed him, at the lodging place
on the road, at the Feast of Booths

why: The Ge'ez məṣlal means a shade or shelter (it is also the word for the booths of the Feast of Booths), so the Plain English Translation renders "the shelter" and leaves the hard word before it unexpressed. Charles 1902 called the Ethiopic here "hopelessly corrupt": his manuscript c reads "on the feast of tabernacles," which he took as an attempt to fix it, and a, b and d made no sense to him. He followed the Latin, which matches the Hebrew of Exodus 4:24, "at the place where they camped for the night."

p: Nothing names what struck the firstborn. Charles supplied "the death of."

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902

readings.en: and (by the death) of the first-born
readings.plain: and by the death of their firstborn

why: Charles 1902 notes that the words he supplied are wanting in both the Ethiopic and the Latin, and takes this as a gap in the Greek version. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez and lets "struck them ... in their firstborn" carry the sense, which Exodus 12:29 makes plain.

a: for you to do before it was done
p: The Ge'ez says Moses was to "do" each plague before it happened. Charles changed one letter to read "announce."

readings.orig: ከመ ፡ ትግበር ፡ ዘእንበለ ፡ ይትገበር (kämä təgbär zäʾnəbälä yətgäbär)
readings.en: that you do (it) before it was done
readings.plain: for you to do before it was done

readings.en: that you should declare (these things) before they were done
readings.plain: for you to announce before it was done

why: VanderKam's Ge'ez reads təgbär, "you do." Charles 1902 corrected it to təngär, "you tell," because "do it before it happened" seems odd, and notes the same confusion of the two verbs in three of his four manuscripts at 49:22. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez: Moses' hand did bring the plagues (Exodus 7:19; Exodus 9:22-23), and announcing them is implied.

a: Prince Mastema was not put to shame
p: The Ge'ez has "not." Charles first removed it, then kept it and corrected "until" to "because."

readings.orig: ኢኀፈረ ፡ መኰንነ ፡ መስቴማ ፡ እስከ ፡ ሶበ ፡ ኀየለ (ʾiḫäfärä mäkʷännä mästema ʾəskä sobä ḫäyälä)
readings.en: Prince Mastema was not ashamed, until he grew strong
readings.plain: Prince Mastema was not put to shame

readings.w: Charles's earlier Ethiopic text (without the negative), as he reports it in 1902
readings.en: was put to shame until he took courage
readings.plain: Prince Mastema was put to shame

readings.en: was not put to shame because he took courage
readings.plain: Prince Mastema was not put to shame, because

why: Charles 1902 says he omitted the negative in his text because the sentence "fails to give a good sense," and now thinks the fault lies in "until," a Hebrew עד־אשר miscopied for על־אשר, "because." He also notes that his manuscript a has "took thought" for "took courage." The Ge'ez keeps the negative, and ʾəskä can carry the sense "so far as," so the Plain English Translation follows it; see the note.

a: between you and the Egyptians, and between the Egyptians and Israel
p: The Ge'ez names Moses, the Egyptians and Israel. Charles's text leaves out "you."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts a and b
readings.orig: ማእከሌከ ፡ ወማእከሎሙ ፡ ለግብጽ ፡ ወማእከሎሙ ፡ ለእስራኤል (maʾkälekä wämaʾkälomu lägbəṣ wämaʾkälomu läʾsəraʾel)
readings.en: between you and between the Egyptians and between Israel
readings.plain: between you and the Egyptians, and between the Egyptians and Israel

readings.w: Charles 1902's text (his manuscripts c and d have the words in another place)

why: Charles 1902 left out "between you and," because the manuscripts put it in different places. VanderKam keeps it, and the Plain English Translation follows him. In Exodus 14:19-20 the angel and the cloud stand "between Egypt's camp and Israel's camp."

p: VanderKam's Ge'ez, as transcribed, has "clothes"; Dillmann's Ge'ez (1859) and Charles have "hearts." The two words differ by one letter.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), in the Open Siddur transcription; the EOTC copy agrees
Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1859), page 160 of his edition (Source Library scan, page 174)
Dillmann's notes on the verb: his manuscript T; his manuscript A
readings.en: and they hardened (T); and they were hard (A)

why: "Hardened their hearts" is the phrase of Exodus 14:4, 14:8 and 14:17, and it gives sense; "made their clothing strong" does not. The Ge'ez words ʾälbab (hearts) and ʾälbas (clothes) differ in one letter (ቢ and ሲ). The EOTC copy is not a separate witness here (it agrees with VanderKam almost everywhere in these chapters), so the Plain English Translation takes Dillmann's noun, with Charles. For the verb it keeps the singular "he hardened" of VanderKam's text; Dillmann's notes record plural forms in two of his manuscripts. The next words, "and made them bold," are the same in both editions (wäʾäḫäyälomu, ወአኀየሎሙ). The Plain English Translation of this verse is therefore chosen word by word from two editions; see the next entry.

a: They were made bold by the Lord our God
t: They were made bold, he was made bold, or a plan?
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez has "they were made strong"; Dillmann's has "he was made strong." Charles's English reads "the device was devised."

readings.orig: ወተኀየሉ ፡ እምኀበ ፡ እግዚአብሔር ፡ አምላክነ (wätäḫäyälu ʾəmḫäbä ʾəgziʾäbḥer ʾämlaknä)
readings.en: and they were made strong by the Lord our God
readings.plain: They were made bold by the Lord our God

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1859), page 160 (his manuscript T: ወተኀየሎሙ)
readings.plain: And he was made bold by the Lord our God

readings.en: and the device was devised by the Lord our God
readings.plain: The plan was planned by the Lord our God

why: The two Ge'ez editions differ only in the last letter: VanderKam's plural wätäḫäyälu, "they were made strong," and Dillmann's singular wätäḫäyälä, "he was made strong." The plural follows on from "made them bold" just before and says plainly who was strengthened, so the Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam here while it takes Dillmann's "hearts" earlier in the verse. Charles's "the device was devised" has no note. At 48:12 he records that his manuscript a reads halaja, "took thought," for hajjala, "took courage": the same two verbs with letters swapped, and a reading of that kind could lie behind his English here.

p: Charles's manuscripts differ: the fourteenth, the fifteenth, or the seventeenth.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscript b; Cedrenus's Greek, as cited in Charles 1902 ("τῇ ιδ'")
readings.orig: ወአመ ፡ ዐሡር ፡ ወረቡዕ ፡ ዕለት (wäʾämä ʿäśur wäräbuʿ ʿəlät)

why: The fourteenth fits the story: the plunder happened before Israel left (Exodus 12:35-36), on the Passover day. Charles 1902 notes that the "seventeenth" of a and d is a one-letter slip (sabuʿ for rabuʿ), and that the chronicler Cedrenus, quoting this passage, has "the fourteenth."

a: For no bone of the Israelites will be crushed.
p: The Latin reads "there will be no trouble among the Israelites on this day." Charles followed it.

readings.orig: እስመ ፡ ኢይትቀጠቀጥ ፡ እምውሉደ ፡ እስራኤል ፡ ምንተሂ ፡ ዐጽም (ʾəsmä ʾiytəqäṭäqäṭ ʾəmwəludä ʾəsraʾel məntähi ʿäṣm)
readings.en: for no bone of the children of Israel will be crushed
readings.plain: For no bone of the Israelites will be crushed.

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.orig: Non erit tribulatio in filiis Istrahel in die hac
readings.en: there will be no trouble among the children of Israel on this day
readings.plain: For there will be no trouble among the Israelites on this day.

why: Charles 1902 thought the Latin right and the Ethiopic corrupt; he suggested that a Hebrew phrase for "on this very day" (be-ʿetsem ha-yom ha-zeh, with ʿetsem, "bone," used for "very") was misread as "bone." That is a clever but uncertain guess. The Ge'ez makes sense as a reason for the rule just given, and is followed. Either way, 49:15 promises Israel safety when the feast is kept rightly.

p: The Ge'ez says "cooked in the fire." The Latin and Charles have "you will eat it."

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902 ("comedetis illud")

why: Charles 1902 called the Ge'ez bəsulä "unmeaning" and replaced it with "they shall eat it" from the Latin. In VanderKam's text it reads naturally as "cooked," beside "roasted," and is followed. The sense of the passage is the same: roast it, and do it with care.

a: Tell them its year, every year, and its day among the days
p: Charles marks "and the day of its days" as corrupt and prefers the Latin "at the time of its days."

readings.orig: ዓመቶ ፡ ለለ ፡ ዓመት ፡ ወዕለቶ ፡ ለዕለታት (ʿamäto lälä ʿamät wäʿläto läʿlätat)
readings.en: its year for each year, and its day for the days
readings.plain: Tell them its year, every year, and its day among the days

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.en: in the time of its days
readings.plain: Tell them every year, during its days

why: Charles 1902 daggers "and the day of its days" as corrupt and thinks the Latin "most probably right"; his manuscripts a and b agree with the Ge'ez "its year every year," while c and d read "every year." The Ge'ez can be read as it stands, so the Plain English Translation follows it; the sense is the same: the feast's date is fixed every year.

p: The Ge'ez says "Sinai"; Charles corrected it to "Sin," as in Exodus 16:1.
why: Charles 1902 writes "Sin[ai] is corrupt for Sin": a wilderness "between Elim and Sinai" cannot itself be Sinai, and Exodus 16:1 names the Wilderness of Sin. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez and explains the slip in a note.
